Notices

The harbour committee meets on the first Monday of the month in the long room of the customs house. The meeting is open to anyone who keeps a boat in the harbour, and the minutes are pinned to the board at the end of the quay.

The quay will be closed to carts on the mornings of the spring tides while the steps are repaired. Boats are asked to land their catch at the slipway on those mornings, and to keep clear of the masons' raft.

The museum asks anyone who has letters, photographs or log books from the light to bring them to the long room on a Sunday afternoon. Nothing will be kept without leave, and everything lent will be copied and returned.

The schoolmistress will give a reading from the record of the lamp-keepers in the long room on the night of the gale. The old lamp will be lit, and the reading ends when its oil runs out.
Moorings in the inner harbour are let by the year from the first of April. A mooring not paid for by the end of April is let to the next boat on the list, which the harbour master keeps.

The new light is shown from sunset to sunrise, and in fog by day. Its character is two white flashes every ten seconds, seen for eighteen miles in clear weather. The old light at the point is no longer shown.
Boats coming in on the evening tide are asked to show their lights from the point at Ardmore, and to keep to the line of the leading marks until they are inside the harbour wall.
The chandlery on the quay has the spring list of prices, and orders for rope, paint and oilskins taken before the end of March are delivered by the first boat in April.
The coal boat is expected in the second week of the month. Coal ordered at the harbour office before it comes is delivered from the quay at the boat's price.
The committee thanks everyone who helped to carry the lifeboat up the slipway after the storm in January, and the women of the town who kept the crew in tea through the night.

The regatta will be held on the last Saturday of July. Entries for the rowing races close at the harbour office a week before, and the swimming race is open to anyone who can swim the width of the harbour.

The ferry to the islands sails on Tuesdays and Fridays from Easter, at nine from the end of the quay, and returns on the evening tide. Tickets are sold on board, and cattle travel at the owner's risk.
Fishermen are asked not to leave their nets to dry on the railings of the quay, which have been painted. The drying poles behind the fish market are free to use.
The postmistress asks that letters for the evening post be in the box at the harbour office by five, so that they go with the mail cart to the station.
The school will close for the herring season from the first of August, and open again when the boats come home. Children are asked to take care on the quay while the boats are landing.
The doctor holds a surgery in the long room every Thursday morning, and visits the islands on the first Friday of the month when the ferry sails.
The library in the customs house lends books for a fortnight, and has a shelf of the Gazette since its first number, which may be read in the room but not taken away.
The harbour master asks owners to look over their moorings before the autumn gales, and to report a worn chain or a dragging anchor at the harbour office before it parts.
The bell at the end of the quay is rung at noon every day, and three times when the harbour master calls the boats in. It is not to be rung for any other reason, by anyone.
